strengths: The manuscript identifies a meaningful limitation of conventional RVOS: relational expressions may require distinguishing the initiator and recipient of an interaction rather than localizing an isolated object.

InterRVOS-8K is substantial in scale, with 8,738 videos, 35,247 objects, 127,314 expressions, and 17,682 actor-target interactions. Its inclusion of role-reversed expressions, motion-only descriptions, and multi-instance references could support useful future research.
The automatic annotation pipeline is described relatively transparently, including the prompts and the use of GPT-4o and LLaMA-3.1-70B at different stages.

The empirical study includes caption-type breakdowns and cross-dataset zero-shot evaluation. Under the shared Sa2VA baseline, InterRVOS-5K training improves zero-shot performance over Ref-SAV on MeViS, Ref-Youtube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS, providing some evidence that the generated data transfer beyond the proposed benchmark.

Joint actor-target prediction is simple and practically useful. ReVIOSa-1B achieves 59.7 overall J&F compared with 53.8 for Sa2VA-1B on the proposed evaluation set, while the reported token ablation favors joint prediction over independent role supervision.
weaknesses: The central dataset-quality claim is not adequately validated. All expressions and interaction labels appear to be generated and verified by language models, but the paper reports no human audit, inter-annotator study, precision of interaction detection, actor/target assignment accuracy, caption grounding accuracy, or comparison against manually written expressions. The examples themselves contain conspicuous errors or unnatural relations, such as “person handing to person,” “Person explaining to person and car,” and a dog described as licking a hand when an ice-cream cone appears central. Because the evaluation annotations are produced by the same pipeline, high scores may reflect agreement with its artifacts rather than genuine interaction understanding.

The new evaluation protocol is materially underspecified. The manuscript does not formally define how actor and target predictions are matched and aggregated, especially for one-to-many interactions. It is also unclear how single-mask baselines such as ReferFormer and LMPM produce the two role-specific predictions scored in Table 5. The paper alternately describes the task as using paired complementary expressions and as producing both masks from one expression, leaving the actual input-output contract ambiguous. Consequently, the main actor-target comparison cannot be reliably interpreted.

Evidence for the architectural claim is weak. ReVIOSa largely adds two special tokens to an existing MLLM-plus-SAM2 framework. Table 6 does not isolate whether the 5.3-point gain comes from joint relational reasoning, additional mask supervision, different output cardinality, or implementation differences. There is no controlled ablation for actor-target supervision, role swapping, target-mask loss, or interaction data, and no comparison with a straightforward multi-object/two-query adaptation of the same backbone.

Evaluation on the proposed test set is not independent of the automatic construction procedure, and no manually verified interaction test subset is provided. Standard benchmarks assess only conventional RVOS, where the proposed architecture is sometimes worse than the shared Sa2VA baseline—for example, 59.3 versus 61.8 on Ref-Youtube-VOS and 63.7 versus 67.1 on Ref-DAVIS. Thus the external results support the value of the training data more strongly than the claimed interaction-aware architecture.

Experimental specification is insufficient for reproducibility: exact train/validation splits and sample counts used in each table, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, LoRA configuration, loss weights, frame sampling, spatial resolution, inference procedure, baseline training recipes, and adaptation of baselines to actor-target output are missing. The project-page URL is also blank in the reviewed manuscript. These are substantive omissions rather than presentation refinements. Several claims are overstated or internally inconsistent. The paper calls the dataset “high-quality” without annotation-quality evidence, describes 127K expressions as 127K “samples,” and inconsistently attributes the dataset construction to VidOR while citing YFCC100M in one location. These reporting issues reinforce uncertainty about the dataset provenance and statistics.

Overall, the task direction and dataset scale are worthwhile, but the lack of validated ground truth and the ambiguity of the principal evaluation prevent the reported numbers from establishing the claimed interaction understanding. These concerns affect the scientific foundation of the contribution and currently outweigh its merits.

strengths: The manuscript identifies a useful gap in RVOS: expressions whose resolution depends on relationships between multiple entities. Explicitly predicting masks for both referred and interacting entities could support interaction-centric video understanding. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/503e63868b1f4feeab9f0761611802c9/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

InterRVOS-8K is substantial in nominal scale, containing 8,738 videos, 35,247 objects, 127,314 expressions, and 17,682 actor-target interactions. The four-stage annotation pipeline and full prompts are documented in considerable detail.

There is encouraging evidence that the data can transfer beyond the proposed benchmark. With the same Sa2VA baseline, InterRVOS-5K obtains zero-shot J&F scores of 41.8 on MeViS-valid, 61.8 on Ref-Youtube-VOS, and 67.1 on Ref-DAVIS, compared with 32.8, 54.2, and 62.1 for Ref-SAV training.

The proposed model is computationally pragmatic, fine-tuning only LoRA modules and the SAM2 decoder. On the authors' benchmark, ReVIOSa-1B improves overall J&F from 53.8 for Sa2VA-1B to 59.7, while the reported ablation favors joint actor-target training over single-token and independently supervised variants.
weaknesses: The central semantic formulation is internally inconsistent. The paper alternates between 'actor' meaning the causal initiator and meaning the grammatical/referred subject. For example, in 'child getting styled by adult,' the child is shown as [SEG_ACT] even though the adult performs the action. This contradicts the claimed actor-target semantics and the Stage-4 prompt, which defines the subject as the performer. Consequently, it is unclear what roles the tokens and annotations consistently represent.

The automatically generated dataset receives no reported human validation. There is no audited sample, correctness rate, inter-annotator agreement, or breakdown of errors in interaction detection, directionality, referential uniqueness, or caption-mask correspondence. Visible examples already contain malformed or semantically weak captions such as 'Person holding for black and brown dog and medium-sized dog' and 'person handing to person.' Thus, scale does not establish annotation quality, and the test labels are not an independent ground truth because they are generated through the same pipeline as the training annotations.

A crucial part of dataset construction is missing: the manuscript does not explain how dense segmentation mask tracks are obtained or validated. It states that the dataset is built on VidOR, but VidOR is ordinarily described through tracked boxes and visual-relation annotations; the paper neither documents a box-to-mask procedure nor reports mask quality. It also inconsistently cites Thomee et al.'s YFCC100M paper as VidOR in Section 3. This omission directly affects the validity and reproducibility of the segmentation benchmark.

The actor-target evaluation protocol is inadequately defined. The paper says it applies standard RVOS evaluation to interaction samples forming expression pairs, but does not specify whether J and F average both simultaneously predicted masks, score only the referred mask, or require correct role assignment as a pair. No actor-versus-target scores, pair-level success metric, or role-confusion analysis is provided. Therefore, Tables 5 and 6 do not convincingly substantiate the central claim of correct joint role-aware segmentation.

Most headline evidence is measured on the authors' automatically generated and deliberately interaction-enriched evaluation set. This favors models trained on matching captions and annotation artifacts. The standard-benchmark zero-shot results support the usefulness of the data, but ReVIOSa itself is worse than the Sa2VA baseline on three of four reported conventional evaluations, including Ref-Youtube-VOS and Ref-DAVIS, weakening claims of broadly improved video understanding.

Comparison conditions are not sufficiently specified. Table 5 does not clearly state the training data and identical optimization conditions used for every competing method, while the construction and sampling of the 2K/5K subsets are omitted. Results are reported from apparently single runs without variance. These issues make architectural and data-quality conclusions difficult to separate from training-budget or sampling effects.

The architectural novelty is limited to introducing two segmentation tokens and joint supervision on top of InternVL, Sa2VA-style grounding, and SAM2. The paper gives no formal model or loss equations and omits essential implementation details such as optimizer, learning rate, frame sampling, input resolution, inference procedure, and loss weights. The displayed project-page URL is blank, and no code, data-access, licensing, or release information is supplied.

Overall, the task direction and transfer results are worthwhile, but the unresolved role-definition contradiction, absent validation of automatically generated language and masks, and underdefined central evaluation prevent the reported numbers from convincingly supporting the paper's main claims. These are material scientific issues rather than presentation refinements, so the balance favors rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of conventional referring video object segmentation: relational expressions often identify an actor through another entity, yet benchmarks supervise only the referred actor. Requiring distinct actor and target masks is a useful and reasonably original extension with relevance to interaction-centric video understanding.

InterRVOS-8K is substantial in scale: 8,738 videos, 35,247 objects, 127,314 expressions, and 17,682 actor-target interactions. It also covers appearance, motion-only, multi-instance, and interaction expressions, making the dataset potentially valuable beyond the proposed baseline.

The four-stage annotation pipeline is clearly motivated, and the appendix provides unusually detailed prompts for caption generation, grouping, interaction discovery, and role assignment. This improves transparency and supports partial reproducibility.

The empirical evidence is encouraging. With the same Sa2VA baseline, InterRVOS-5K improves zero-shot performance over Ref-SAV on MeViS valid from 32.8 to 41.8 J&F and also gives the best transfer results on Ref-Youtube-VOS and Ref-DAVIS. This indicates that the benefit is not confined to the proposed test set.

ReVIOSa is a simple, appropriate baseline that extends a SAM2/MLLM system with separate actor and target tokens. It obtains the best overall InterRVOS-8K result, while the joint-token ablation improves J&F from 54.4 to 59.7 over independently trained role tokens. Qualitative examples further show plausible separation of interacting entities.
weaknesses: The most important limitation is the absence of a human audit of the automatically generated annotations. The paper reports no sampled precision, role-assignment accuracy, caption correctness, inter-annotator agreement, or comparison against human annotations. This matters because GPT-4o both detects interactions and decides their direction, and visible examples contain awkward or questionable expressions such as "person holding for ... dog" and "person explaining to person and car." Dataset scale alone does not establish annotation quality.

The actor-target evaluation protocol is underspecified. It is not clear how scores from the two output masks are matched and aggregated, how one-to-many targets are represented, or how missing/spurious role tokens are penalized. The unusually higher Actor-Target scores than standard Referring scores may simply reflect category difficulty, so they do not by themselves demonstrate stronger relational reasoning.

Baseline comparison details are incomplete. Table 5 does not clearly state the training data and adaptation protocol for every method, and it is unclear whether all competing models receive equivalent actor-target supervision, optimization budgets, and output capacity. Since existing models were not designed to emit two role-specific masks, this information is necessary to interpret the claimed state of the art fairly.

The ablation evidence does not isolate all relevant factors. The paper compares one token, independently supervised role tokens, and joint role tokens, but does not test matched multi-mask capacity without semantic roles, shuffled actor-target assignments, interaction captions without target-mask supervision, or performance specifically on role-reversal pairs. Thus, the large gain supports joint multi-entity supervision but does not conclusively show that the model learned interaction semantics rather than benefiting from additional masks and supervision.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript specifies model backbones, epochs, batch size, hardware, and prompts, but omits optimizer, learning rate and schedule, LoRA rank and placement, frame sampling, input resolution, loss weights, decoding rules, dataset filtering thresholds, and enough detail to recreate the splits exactly. The project-page URL is also absent in the submitted PDF.

Some claims are overstated or imprecise. The method is described alternately as operating on paired expressions and as producing both entities from a single expression; the distinction between the task definition, training instances, and evaluation units should be formalized. Likewise, improved segmentation does not directly establish "deeper comprehension" without diagnostics of predicate or role understanding. These are meaningful clarity issues but do not outweigh the dataset's demonstrated utility.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of standard RVOS: interaction expressions often specify asymmetric roles, yet existing formulations return only one referred-object mask. Separately predicting actor and target masks is a useful task direction for relational video understanding.

InterRVOS-127K is potentially valuable in scale and scope: it contains 127,236 expressions over 8,738 videos, including 17,604 actor-target interaction expressions, and the evaluation subset is reportedly human-corrected.

ReVIOSa is conceptually simple and relevant to the task. Dedicated actor/target tokens provide explicit role-conditioned outputs, while attention-mask supervision offers a plausible way to improve visual grounding.

The reported results are promising. ReVIOSa-4B obtains 74.5 actor and 68.3 target J&F on the proposed benchmark, and the dataset-transfer experiments show improvements over Ref-SAV training on MeViS despite fewer samples. The appendix provides annotation prompts, compute requirements, attention visualizations, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: Material concern: the benchmark's annotation reliability is insufficiently established. Training masks are automatically produced with SAM2 and interaction labels with GPT-4o/LLaMA, but there is no quantitative audit of mask accuracy, interaction correctness, role correctness, or caption grounding. For the human-corrected evaluation set, the paper omits annotator counts, correction instructions, quality-control procedures, agreement statistics, and the number of interaction samples. These omissions are consequential because the dataset is the central contribution.

Material concern: evaluation-set reuse appears likely. The paper describes only training and evaluation sets, while layer selection and the top-k-head choice are chosen empirically using segmentation performance (Tables 3 and Figure 7). No separate validation split is identified. If these choices used the reported evaluation set, the principal results are affected by model-selection leakage.

The main comparison does not convincingly isolate the proposed method's benefit. Existing methods are simply marked inapplicable for target segmentation rather than being adapted through two role-specific prompts, two passes, or separate actor/target heads. The paper also does not clearly state whether every Table 2 baseline was retrained on exactly the same InterRVOS data and settings. Consequently, the claimed state of the art on a newly introduced task is weakly supported.

The key ablation is not aligned with the central claim. Table 4 reports a single score whose full-model value, 62.0, matches the standard RVOS column in Table 2 rather than either actor or target performance. It therefore does not directly show that specialized tokens or AML improve target segmentation, actor-target separation, or resistance to role swapping. No confusion/swap metric or evaluation on minimally reversed expressions is provided.

The task semantics and metric require sharper specification. The pipeline generates passive role-reversed expressions, making grammatical subject, semantic agent, and the paper's term 'actor' potentially different; examples such as an object 'being led by' another object expose this ambiguity. Multi-target interactions are also included, but the paper does not precisely explain whether a role mask is a union, how absent or symmetric roles are handled, or how J&F is aggregated in these cases.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the extensive appendix. Missing details include optimizer and learning rate, loss weights, LoRA configuration, SAM2 variant, input resolution and frame sampling, baseline-training recipes, split construction at source-video level, and exact metric aggregation. The manuscript also overstates conclusions such as improved understanding of inter-object dynamics when the evidence primarily demonstrates segmentation gains on labels generated by the same pipeline. Numerous grammatical errors are a secondary presentation issue, but not the reason for the rejection recommendation.

strengths: The actor/target formulation is a useful extension of RVOS: separately segmenting asymmetric interaction roles is more informative than returning only an actor mask or the union of all involved objects.

InterRVOS-127K is potentially valuable in scale and scope, with 127,236 expressions over 8,738 videos and 17,604 actor-target interaction expressions. The 738-video evaluation portion is reportedly corrected by human annotators.
ReVIOSa is conceptually simple and well matched to the task. Separate actor and target tokens enable both masks in one pass, while the attention-mask loss provides an explicit grounding signal.

The paper includes component ablations, attention analyses, dataset comparisons, conventional RVOS results, and zero-shot evaluations. The reported improvements from role tokens and AML are meaningful on the authors' benchmark.
weaknesses: The central evaluation does not establish a fair comparison. Existing methods have no InterRVOS-Target results, and the paper does not compare against straightforward actor-target baselines such as two-pass prompting, expression rewriting, or an otherwise matched two-token Sa2VA variant. Consequently, the claimed state of the art on the newly introduced task is largely uncontested.

The manuscript does not clearly state whether every Table 2 baseline was retrained on exactly the same InterRVOS-127K training split, with comparable inputs and optimization. Without this information, the actor/RVOS gains cannot be confidently attributed to interaction modeling rather than training-data or implementation differences.

The only described evaluation set is also used for extensive ablations and design selection. Table 3 selects the number of supervised heads by J&F, Figure 7 compares candidate layers, and the final result is then reported on apparently the same set. No independent validation/test split or hidden test is documented, creating material model-selection bias.

Dataset reliability is insufficiently validated. Training masks and captions are automatically produced using SAM2, GPT-4o, and LLaMA, yet the paper reports no manual audit size, mask quality, caption correctness, actor-target agreement, correction rate, annotator count, or inter-annotator agreement. Human correction is asserted only for the evaluation set. Examples such as "dish feeding person and child" also expose awkward or semantically questionable role reversal.

The benchmark construction lacks essential safeguards and statistics: it is unclear whether clips derived from the same long VidOR source can cross splits, how many of the 5,048 evaluation expressions are actor-target cases, how interaction types and categories are distributed, and how performance varies by ambiguity, object count, interaction direction, or target size.

The evaluation averages actor and target segmentation separately but provides no joint per-interaction metric that requires both roles to be correct simultaneously, no actor-target swap/confusion analysis, and no accuracy for deciding whether an expression is interactive and emitting one versus two tokens. These omissions leave the main role-understanding claim only partially tested.

The AML formulation is underspecified and technically questionable: attention weights normalized over many visual and text tokens are supervised with dense binary BCE, but the paper does not explain aggregation or normalization, class imbalance, or how a probability distribution can match a multi-positive mask. The correlation analysis is observational and may largely reflect object size; relevant controls are absent.

Reproducibility is poor. Learning rate, optimizer, LoRA configuration, loss weights, frame counts, spatial resolutions, prompts, data preprocessing, and most inference details are missing, and the project-page URL is blank. These are not merely stylistic refinements because they prevent replication of both the dataset and model results.

Overall, the task and dataset idea have merit, but the lack of a clean held-out protocol, matched actor-target baselines, and quantitative annotation-quality evidence prevents the reported numbers from convincingly supporting the paper's main claims. These are consequential scientific weaknesses rather than presentation issues.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of standard RVOS and formulates a useful extension: separately segmenting actors and targets captures directional interactions that a single referred-object mask cannot represent.

InterRVOS-127K is potentially valuable infrastructure. It contains 127,236 expressions over 8,738 videos, including 17,604 actor-target interaction expressions, and the authors provide the complete staged annotation prompts, dataset statistics, and human refinement of the evaluation set.

ReVIOSa is technically coherent: role-specific [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens map naturally to the task, while attention mask loss supplies explicit spatial grounding. The approach integrates cleanly with an MLLM and SAM2 rather than requiring an unnecessarily elaborate architecture.

The empirical results are encouraging. ReVIOSa-4B obtains 74.5 actor and 68.3 target J&F on the new benchmark, while the 1B variant exceeds the tested actor-only baselines on actor segmentation. Results on MeViS, Ref-Youtube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS also show that interaction-oriented training remains competitive outside the proposed setting.

The component ablation reports gains from both role-specific tokens and AML, and the layer/head studies, attention visualizations, dataset-size controls, and zero-shot evaluations provide useful supporting evidence beyond a single headline comparison.
The manuscript is well organized and visually clear. Its task definition, annotation pipeline, architecture, and qualitative actor-target outputs are easy to understand.
weaknesses: The reliability of the new benchmark is insufficiently quantified. Although the 5,048-expression evaluation set is said to be human-refined, the paper does not report the number of annotators, correction rate, annotation protocol, quality-control process, or inter-annotator agreement. This matters because the expressions, interaction direction, and initial SAM2 mask tracks all originate from an automated pipeline.

There is no substantive target-segmentation baseline. Existing methods are marked inapplicable rather than adapted, for example by separately prompting them with actor- and target-specific referring phrases or training comparable two-output variants. Consequently, the 68.3 target J&F establishes an absolute result but not how much ReVIOSa improves over reasonable alternatives.

The main architectural ablation reports only a single J&F value that matches the overall RVOS result, not separate actor and target scores. It therefore does not directly establish that [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] or AML improves target localization and role disambiguation, which are the central claims.

The AML formulation needs greater technical justification. Transformer attention is normalized across tokens, yet binary cross-entropy pushes every foreground patch toward one; this objective depends on object area and is not obviously compatible with attention normalization. The empirical gains help, but comparisons with normalized mask distributions or alternative grounding losses are absent.

Several dataset-effect comparisons remain confounded. Table A3 compares datasets with substantially different expression counts, while the better-controlled Table A2 is limited to MeViS. It is also unclear whether clips derived from the same original VidOR video are guaranteed not to cross training and evaluation splits.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the loss weights, learning rate and schedule, optimizer, LoRA configuration, frame-sampling parameters, inference thresholds, and exact evaluation-set interaction count are not reported. The manuscript also does not clearly state concrete release terms for the generated masks, annotations, and training code.

The claimed scale should be contextualized more carefully: only 17,604 of the 127,236 expressions are actor-target interactions, and mirrored active/passive captions can increase expression counts without adding new visual instances. The task-specific portion is still useful, but smaller than the headline dataset name suggests.
